items.prompt: Discuss how to phase two fictional regional-trade improvements. Coordinated documents can reduce delays at existing border facilities sooner and at lower cost. A funded freight-link upgrade serves more producers but takes two years. Both have agreed maintenance or operating responsibilities; resources cover one first.
items.canonical_answer: Document coordination offers earlier savings for existing traders and uses fewer resources. The freight link can widen participation beyond those traders, but its benefits take longer and commit more funds. Prioritise coordination where present administrative delay is the main obstacle; choose the link where excluded producers face much larger transport barriers. Judge actual reach, timing and costs, and retain a route to the second improvement. An agreement alone does not establish those outcomes.
marking_guidance: Judgement: compare genuine benefits and costs against the stated aim.
Reason: develop each option using supplied evidence, weigh the trade-off, and give a conditional conclusion.

items.prompt: Describe this fictional corridor comparison: A has low tariffs but deliveries take ten days with repeated bridge closures; B has similar tariffs and maintained links with four-day delivery.
items.canonical_answer: B combines maintained physical access with delivery six days faster despite similar tariffs. The contrast indicates that tariff arrangements alone do not describe practical market access.
marking_guidance: Evidence: use tariff similarity and delivery times.
Relationship: connect access conditions to the observed contrast without isolating all causes.

items.prompt: Discuss which fictional SACU-related support to phase first. Joint document assistance would reduce frequent delivery delays for existing producers. Quality training would help smaller producers qualify for buyers but takes longer. Both operate within common customs arrangements and are feasible.
items.canonical_answer: Document support helps existing sellers turn common-market access into more dependable deliveries quickly. Quality training expands the set of producers able to benefit, but brings less immediate relief. Prefer document assistance where delays threaten current sales; prefer training where exclusion through quality is the larger development gap. Assess the distribution as well as the size of gains. Common customs rules provide an opportunity without guaranteeing either reliable trade or equal participation.

items.prompt: Discuss a fictional SADC transport project. Joint construction and funded maintenance can connect more markets, but cost-sharing commits resources that each state could use for smaller domestic routes. States agree roles; benefits are expected to be larger near the cross-border corridor.
items.canonical_answer: A joint route can overcome a bottleneck that separate national projects leave in place, widening trade and shared service opportunities. It also uses scarce public funds and may concentrate benefits near the corridor. Support it where expected cross-border gains justify those costs and less-connected communities have a credible access plan. Domestic routes may be preferable where local needs outweigh the marginal regional gain. Funded responsibilities improve feasibility but do not prove an equitable outcome.

items.prompt: Discuss which support best helps fictional exporters use an EU-partner trade opportunity. Both have compliant products. A marketing programme would reach more buyers for existing large firms. A quality-training programme would help smaller suppliers maintain compliance but reach fewer export orders initially. Both have feasible finance.
items.canonical_answer: Marketing may convert existing capacity into sales sooner, using firms already able to comply and deliver. Training can broaden participation and reduce future quality failures, but initial sales may be smaller. Prefer training where lasting local supplier capability and inclusion are priorities; marketing may better serve urgent earnings from established capacity. Check cost, retained local gains and actual orders, rather than assuming agreement access makes every firm competitive.

items.prompt: State (a) one distinction between SACU and SADC [2]. Explain (b) why fictional tariff cooperation without a functioning bridge may not deliver the intended regional market gains [4].
items.canonical_answer: (a) SACU is a customs union with common customs arrangements; SADC has a broader regional development and integration scope. (b) Tariff cooperation can reduce the charges on qualifying regional goods, making exchange more attractive. The broken physical connection still prevents those goods reaching buyers, so lower charges alone cannot create the intended deliveries. Without deliveries, producers cannot realise the expected market access or sales gains from the agreement. A feasible maintained transport connection and workable border implementation must complement the tariff arrangement; judge actual participation and delivered trade rather than agreement signing alone.
marking_guidance: Point: two correctly paired institutional features [2].
Development: link tariff opportunity and physical constraint to the practical result [4].
Original indicative practice guidance; not an official mark scheme.

items.prompt: Describe (a) this fictional comparison under similar trade terms: A’s deliveries take eight days and 30% arrive late; B’s take three days and 5% late [3]. Suggest (b) a priority for A if unreliable road access is documented and the aim is dependable sales [3].
items.canonical_answer: (a) A combines five more delivery days with a late share 25 points higher. (b) Address the documented road reliability with responsible providers and maintenance, then monitor delivery; identical agreement terms do not resolve unequal practical access.

Meaning: match an implementable priority to the actual barrier and aim [3].
